The patient presents with classic fluctuating, activity-dependent symptoms of myasthenia gravis (MG): diplopia, proximal limb weakness (difficulty climbing stairs, brushing hair), and fatigability with improvement after rest. Laboratory testing confirms elevated acetylcholine receptor antibodies (AChR-Ab = 9 nmol/L — above typical cutoff of >0.4–0.6 nmol/L), strongly supporting autoimmune MG. Repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) shows decremental response in both distal (abductor digiti minimi) and proximal (trapezius) muscles — a hallmark electrophysiological feature of postsynaptic NMJ transmission failure. **Clinical Diagnosis:** Generalized Myasthenia Gravis (AChR antibody–positive, non-thymomatous)  

**Key Supporting Evidence:**
